The product rule. One of three essential differentiation rules alongside the power rule and chain rule. The derivative of a product of two functions equals the derivative of the first times the second, plus the first times the derivative of the second. When you differentiate expressions with two multiplied functions, such as x times sine of x or e to the x times the quantity x squared plus one, you need the product rule. Formally: the derivative with respect to x of f of x times g of x equals f prime of x times g of x plus f of x times g prime of x. A helpful mnemonic is "first times derivative of second, plus second times derivative of first." Crucially, this is not the same as the product of the derivatives. The derivative of f times g is not equal to the derivative of f times the derivative of g. Some examples: the derivative of x times sine of x simplifies to sine of x plus x cosine of x. The derivative of e to the x times the quantity x squared plus one simplifies to e to the x times the quantity x squared plus two x plus one. The derivative of x times ln of x simplifies to ln of x plus one. The quotient rule is the analogous rule for division: if h equals f divided by g, then h prime equals f prime times g minus f times g prime, all divided by g squared. The product rule generalizes to products of three or more functions. For f times g times h, the derivative equals f prime times g times h plus f times g prime times h plus f times g times h prime. When combining the product rule with the chain rule for composite products, such as the derivative of sine of x times e to the two x, you must apply both rules systematically. The product rule is foundational in calculus, appearing frequently combined with the chain rule in complex differentiation problems.
